name: AnimatedCrossFade
summary: Flutter's `AnimatedCrossFade`: fades between two children while its size goes from the one's to the other's.
doc:
Flutter's `AnimatedCrossFade`: fades between two children while its size
goes from the one's to the other's.

```dart
Watch(panel.open, builder: (open) => AnimatedCrossFade(
  firstChild: const Text('Show more'),
  secondChild: Details(item),
  crossFadeState: open ? CrossFadeState.showSecond : CrossFadeState.showFirst,
  duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 250),
))
```

Both children are always in the page, and switching [crossFadeState]
only changes their classes (that is what a `Watch` swaps in the
browser): the shown one is in the flow and sets the size, the other
fades out over it, then leaves the accessibility tree and the tab order
(`visibility`), so `excludeBottomFocus` is always true. Switching fast
back and forth (A → B → A) reverses from the opacity and the height it
has at that moment.

`// web:` [alignment] is vertical only; the size animates like
[AnimatedSize] (otherwise it changes at once while the fade still runs in
CSS); [onEnd] (not in Flutter) and `animateWidth` are those of
[AnimatedSize]. With a [layoutBuilder] the hidden child stays where the
builder puts it (Flutter's default puts it over the shown one): it fades
and leaves the accessibility tree and the tab order all the same.

name: AnimatedList
summary: Flutter's `AnimatedList`: a list whose rows animate when they come in and when they go out.
doc:
Flutter's `AnimatedList`: a list whose rows animate when they come in
and when they go out.

It is a [Watch.list]: change the list in the state and the browser adds,
moves and removes the rows by their key; this animates the two ends. A
row that enters starts from the first value of its [itemBuilder]'s
animation and goes to the last; one that leaves goes back before it is
removed. Each row is built **once** on the server, so the animation is a
CSS transition, never a Dart frame:

```dart
AnimatedList<Note, int>(
  notes.items.call,
  itemKey: notes.idOf,
  duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 250),
  itemBuilder: (context, row, animation) => SizeTransition(
    sizeFactor: CurvedAnimation(parent: animation, curve: Curves.easeOut),
    child: FadeTransition(
      opacity: animation,
      child: ListTile(
        title: row.text(notes.titleOf),
        trailing: IconButton(
          onPressed: notes.remove.withArg(row.key),
          icon: const Icon(Icons.delete),
        ),
      ),
    ),
  ),
)
```

The rows the page draws the first time (Flutter's `initialItemCount`)
don't animate, and with no JavaScript or with `prefers-reduced-motion`
nothing does: rows just appear and disappear.

`// web:` differences with Flutter's:
- there is no `AnimatedListState` or `GlobalKey`: `insertItem` is adding
  the item to the list of the state and `removeItem` removing it, with
  the state's own methods (`onPressed: notes.remove.withArg(row.key)`);
- [itemBuilder] gets the row (its typed `key`, `row.text`, …) in place of
  the `index`: rows are found by their key;
- the same builder serves a row that enters and one that leaves (Flutter
  takes a `removeItem(…, builder)` for the second), with an `animation`
  that is 1 for a row at rest and 0 where it starts: `animation` is not a
  controller (it has no listeners, and `status` is `completed`), only the
  transition widgets (`FadeTransition`, `ScaleTransition`,
  `SlideTransition`, `SizeTransition`, `RotationTransition`,
  `DecoratedBoxTransition`), `Tween`s, `CurvedAnimation`s and
  `CurveTween`s accept it;
- [duration] is the list's, not each call's;
- a row that leaves stays in the page (inert) for [duration], so a
  `Watch.list` with the same key added again meanwhile shows twice.

})
constructors.summary: Animates the rows of [source] (a `List` of the state: `notes.items.call`, like [Watch.list]), each built by [itemBuilder].

name: AnimatedSize
summary: Flutter's `AnimatedSize`: animates its own size when [child]'s changes.
doc:
Flutter's `AnimatedSize`: animates its own size when [child]'s changes.

```dart
AnimatedSize(
  duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 200),
  curve: Curves.easeOut,
  child: Watch(faq.open, builder: (open) => Text(open ? longAnswer : shortAnswer)),
)
```

The content must change *inside* the widget (a `Watch` below it, a list
that grows): a `Watch` around the whole `AnimatedSize` swaps the element
itself, and there is nothing left to animate. The size follows growing
and shrinking, from zero and back to zero, and a change in the middle of
an animation starts from the height it has then.

`// web:` only the height animates by default (the width is the parent's,
as a block); `animateWidth: true` shrink-wraps the content and animates
both. [alignment] positions the content vertically while it grows or
shrinks (the horizontal part does nothing). [onEnd] runs when the size
animation finishes (not when it is cut short by a newer change; with
`prefers-reduced-motion` it runs right after the instant change). The
measuring and the animation run in the browser: before the page
is interactive the size changes at once.

name: AnimatedSwitcher
summary: Flutter's `AnimatedSwitcher`: animates the switch between the states of the `Watch` it wraps.
doc:
Flutter's `AnimatedSwitcher`: animates the switch between the states
of the `Watch` it wraps.

It adds no element: it marks the `Watch`'s element, and when the
state changes in the browser the engine applies the new state inside a
view transition. The element cross-fades from one state to the next
(or morphs, when both states share it), and every `Hero` inside it
glides from its old place and size to the new one; the rest of the page
changes at once. Around anything that isn't a `Watch` with states it
does nothing.

```dart
AnimatedSwitcher(
  duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 300),
  switchInCurve: Curves.easeInOut,
  child: Watch(layout.isRow, builder: (row) => Flex(
    direction: row ? Axis.horizontal : Axis.vertical,
    children: [for (final l in labels) Hero(tag: 'item-$l', child: Text(l))],
  )),
)
```

It works from either side of the `Watch`: around it (above), or as the
root of its builder (through `Padding` and the like), where the `Watch`
swaps its whole element and the switcher marks that one; deeper in the
builder's tree it marks an element nothing swaps:

```dart
Watch(page.step, builder: (step) => AnimatedSwitcher(
  duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 200),
  child: Text(titles[step]),
))
```

Anywhere else (no `Watch` above or below) it does nothing; the
`animated_switcher_without_watch` lint (THOR-S016) says so while you
write it.

Without view transitions in the browser, with `prefers-reduced-motion`
or without JavaScript, the state changes at once.

`// web:` Flutter keeps both children in a `Stack` and runs
`transitionBuilder` on each; here the browser animates snapshots of
the page, so there is no `transitionBuilder` or `layoutBuilder` (the
animation is always the cross-fade, plus the `Hero`es' moves).
A `Hero` inside the states needs a tag unique in each state (not across
states: the same tag in two states is how an element moves).

})

name: AppBar
summary: Flutter's `AppBar` (Material 3 small top app bar) as one `<header>`: a grid with the [leading] widget, the [title] and the [actions] on the toolbar row, and [bottom] (e.g. a `TabBar`) under it.
doc:
Flutter's `AppBar` (Material 3 small top app bar) as one `<header>`: a
grid with the [leading] widget, the [title] and the [actions] on the
toolbar row, and [bottom] (e.g. a `TabBar`) under it.

Inside `Scaffold(appBar:)` the header is the scaffold's banner landmark
(no extra wrapper) and sticks to the top while the page scrolls, like
Flutter's app bar over a scrolling body.

In a `Scaffold` with a `drawer:`, the bar shows a [DrawerButton] before
the title by itself (and an [EndDrawerButton] after it for an
`endDrawer:`), like Flutter's; [automaticallyImplyLeading] and
[automaticallyImplyActions] turn them off.

```dart
Scaffold(
  appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Sales')),   // + the menu button
  drawer: Drawer(child: Menu()),
  body: …,
)

AppBar(
  leading: DialogTrigger(id: 'menu', child: IconButton(icon: menuIcon, tooltip: 'Menu')),
  title: const Text('Sales'),
  actions: [IconButton(icon: searchIcon, onPressed: search.open, tooltip: 'Search')],
  scrolledUnderElevation: 3,
)
```

summary: Flutter's `Autocomplete<T>` (Material): a text field that suggests [optionsBuilder]'s options as the visitor types, in a panel under it.
doc:
Flutter's `Autocomplete<T>` (Material): a text field that suggests
[optionsBuilder]'s options as the visitor types, in a panel under it.

```dart
Autocomplete<String>(
  optionsBuilder: (value) =>
      fruits.where((f) => f.contains(value.text.toLowerCase())),
  onSelected: order.pickFruit,        // void pickFruit(String fruit)
)
```

is in the top layer under the field, so no `Stack` clips it and no
sibling covers it. Rows are `option`s of a `listbox`; the field is the
`combobox` and announces the highlighted option through
`aria-activedescendant`.

[AutocompleteOptionsBuilder]), and the browser keeps the ones whose text
contains what is typed. For options a server finds as the visitor types
(a store search), use [RawAutocomplete] with a `ThorState` list in
[optionsViewBuilder]. [onSelected] needs a method of a `ThorState` to run
in the browser, and the options encodable as a `ThorState` argument

summary: Flutter's `AutofillGroup`: the fields inside are one group for the browser's autofill and password manager (a login's username and password).
doc:
Flutter's `AutofillGroup`: the fields inside are one group for the
browser's autofill and password manager (a login's username and
password).

```dart
AutofillGroup(
  child: Column(children: [
    TextField(name: 'user', autofillHints: [AutofillHints.username]),
    TextField(name: 'pass', obscureText: true, autofillHints: [AutofillHints.password]),
  ]),
)
```

`// web:` browsers group fields by their `<form>`, so inside a `Form`
(or with a `Form` as its child, Flutter's usual order) the group adds
nothing; outside one it is a `<form autocomplete="on"
method="dialog">` (a submit never navigates, so the password never ends
up in the URL). Inside a dialog it adds no element either: a
`method="dialog"` form there would close the dialog on Enter. A `Form`
deeper below a group that is a `<form>` is an error (a form in a form is
not HTML): make the `Form` the group's child, or the group its child.

of every field inside with `section-<name>`, so two groups on the page
(shipping and billing) are filled apart.

name: Cached
summary: Keeps the HTML of [child] for later requests of the same process: the next page that builds a `Cached` with the same [cacheKey], at the same place, adds the kept HTML instead of building [child] again.
doc:
Keeps the HTML of [child] for later requests of the same process: the
next page that builds a `Cached` with the same [cacheKey], at the same
place, adds the kept HTML instead of building [child] again.

```dart
for (final a in articles)
  Cached(
    // Everything the preview shows: the key *is* its content.
    cacheKey: (a.slug, a.title, a.favorited, a.favoritesCount),
    child: ArticlePreview(a),
  )
```

The contract:

- **[cacheKey] identifies everything [child] shows.** Two pages that
  build the same key get the same HTML, whoever asks: never cache
  something personal under a key that doesn't include whose it is.
  A key made of the values the subtree renders (a record of fields) is
  correct by construction and needs no invalidation.
- **The place is part of the key**: the widgets above (their types) and
  the layout rules of the parent. The inherited values the subtree reads
  (`Theme`, `DefaultTextStyle`, the current route) must be the same for
  every page that uses the key.
- The classes, keyframes and SVG symbols the subtree registered are
  registered again on each page that reuses it, in the same order, so the
  page is byte for byte the one a fresh build gives.
- Not allowed (a `StateError`, in every build mode): a `ThorState` in
  the subtree (its HTML carries per-request values), `Document.head` or
  `<html>`/`<head>`/`<body>` inside, and a wrapper right around
  `Cached` (`Padding`, `Expanded`…: put it inside).
- Entries expire after [ttl] (none: until evicted), are evicted least
  recently used beyond [maxEntries], and are dropped with [invalidate]
  or [clear].

`// web:` Flutter has no equivalent (it never renders HTML twice).
Without a `ThorApp` the child is always built. In debug builds a
subtree inside one of your components is always built too: its classes
are named after the component (`product-card__row`) and the names
depend on the page.

name: CallbackShortcuts
summary: Flutter's `CallbackShortcuts`: key presses inside [child] (while the focus is in it) call methods of a `ThorState`.
doc:
Flutter's `CallbackShortcuts`: key presses inside [child] (while the
focus is in it) call methods of a `ThorState`.

```dart
CallbackShortcuts(
  bindings: {
    const SingleActivator(LogicalKeyboardKey.arrowDown): grid.down,
    const SingleActivator(LogicalKeyboardKey.keyZ, meta: true): grid.undo,
    const SingleActivator(LogicalKeyboardKey.enter): grid.edit.withArg(0),
  },
  child: Focus(child: table),
)
```

Like in Flutter, the innermost matching shortcut wins and stops the
key, and a text field keeps the keys it edits with (letters, arrows,
Backspace); Enter, Escape and Tab still reach the shortcuts around it.
The element needs the focus: wrap it (or a descendant) in [Focus].

**Over a text field:** a binding with `overrideTextInput: true` also
answers when the focus is in a text field and the key is one it edits
with, and the caret does not move (a palette's arrows moving a highlight
while typing). Without it the keys stay in the field.

```dart
CallbackShortcuts(
  bindings: {
    const SingleActivator(LogicalKeyboardKey.arrowDown, overrideTextInput: true): menu.next,
  },
  child: TextField(controller: menu.query),
)
```

Activators: `SingleActivator` (a key and its modifiers) and
`CharacterActivator` (the character typed, whatever keys make it).

**Any character:** [onCharacter] gets every printable character that
no binding of this element took (one character, no Control or Meta):
a grid starts editing the selected cell with the key the user typed,
like a spreadsheet.

```dart
CallbackShortcuts(
  bindings: {const SingleActivator(LogicalKeyboardKey.enter): grid.edit},
  onCharacter: grid.typeInto,   // void typeInto(String character)
  child: Focus(child: table),
)
```

**Nothing focused:** a key pressed while the focus is on the page
itself (`<body>`, as right after it loads) goes to the outermost
`CallbackShortcuts` on view, like Flutter's root focus scope: a ⌘K
declared in a layout works before anything was clicked.

`// web:` decorates [child]'s element instead of adding a
node; a callback that is not a `ThorState` method does nothing. Flutter
has no activator for "any character" (there it is `Focus.onKeyEvent`
reading `KeyEvent.character`, a closure the page can't run):
[onCharacter] is that case as a state method.

A whole number that counts as [count] animates, from where it starts to
where it ends: a figure of a dashboard that fills up. [prefix] and
[suffix] go around it (`' %'`), in [style].

```dart
CountTransition(
  count: IntTween(begin: 0, end: 96).animate(
    CurvedAnimation(parent: controller, curve: Curves.easeOutCubic),
  ),
  suffix: ' %',
)
```

The page holds the final figure as text (it copies, searches and reads
as `96 %`, and it sets the width, so nothing moves); while it counts a
copy on top shows the steps. It plays like the other transitions: at
render, [AnimationController.onVisible] or [AnimationController.inView].

web: the steps are CSS counters, so they are plain digits (no thousands
separator); the final text is [format]ted. A controller of a `ThorState`
shows the figure where it rests, with no count yet.

`SliverFillRemaining`) stacked in one scrolling box.

```dart
CustomScrollView(
  slivers: [
    SliverAppBar(pinned: true, title: Text('Catalog')),
    SliverPadding(
      padding: EdgeInsets.all(16),
      sliver: SliverGrid.extent(maxCrossAxisExtent: 240, children: cards),
```

and a pinned `SliverAppBar` is `position: sticky`: no scroll listeners,
and every item is in the HTML. It scrolls when something gives it a

name: DecoratedBoxTransition
summary: Flutter's `DecoratedBoxTransition`: a [DecoratedBox] whose [decoration] animates.
doc:
Flutter's `DecoratedBoxTransition`: a [DecoratedBox] whose [decoration]
animates.

```dart
DecoratedBoxTransition(
  decoration: DecorationTween(
    begin: BoxDecoration(color: Colors.red, borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(4)),
    end: BoxDecoration(color: Colors.blue, borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(20)),
  ).animate(CurvedAnimation(parent: card.pulse, curve: Curves.easeOut)),
  child: content,
)
```

Each property of the decoration that changes (background color, corner
radius, border, shadows) is a track of keyframes between its two values,
and the browser interpolates it; what stays the same isn't animated. It
plays like the other transitions (a controller of a `ThorState`, at
render, `AnimationController.onVisible`, and as the row animation of an

name: DialogTrigger
summary: Makes its `<button>` child open a dialog (Invoker Commands). Three ways to say which one, the first needing no name at all:
doc:
Makes its `<button>` child open a dialog (Invoker Commands). Three ways
to say which one, the first needing no name at all:

* [dialog]: the dialog travels with its button, like Flutter's
  `onPressed: () => showDialog(builder: …)` reads. The trigger renders
  the button and, right after it, the closed `<dialog>`; the page names
  it.
* [controller]: the dialog that holds the same `DialogController` (a
  field of a `ThorState`).
* [id]: the dialog with that DOM id.

`// web:` the button needs no `onPressed` (Flutter code writes one only
to enable the button): the browser opens the dialog and the button
stays enabled.

The child may also be a tappable box (an `InkWell` or `GestureDetector`
around a card): the browser only runs the command on a `<button>`, so
that element is a focusable `role="button"` and the engine opens the
dialog on a click, Enter or Space. [DialogClose] works the same.

```dart
DialogTrigger(
  dialog: AlertDialog(
    title: const Text('Delete?'),
    actions: [DialogClose(child: TextButton(child: const Text('Cancel')))],
  ),
  child: FilledButton(child: const Text('Delete')),
)
```

name: Dismissible
summary: Flutter's `Dismissible`: a widget that is dismissed by dragging it away.
doc:
Flutter's `Dismissible`: a widget that is dismissed by dragging it away.

```dart
Dismissible(
  key: ValueKey(m.id),
  direction: DismissDirection.endToStart,
  onDismissed: inbox.archived.withArg(m.id),   // void archived(int id, DismissDirection d)
  confirmDismiss: inbox.ask.withArg(m.id),     // Future<bool> ask(int id, DismissDirection d)
  background: const ColoredBox(color: Color(0xFF16A34A)),
  child: MessageTile(m),
)
```

The child follows the pointer (pointer events and a CSS `translate`: the
browser moves it, no Dart per frame) and shows the [background] under it.
Past [dismissThresholds] (a fraction of its size; 0.4 by default) or with a
quick fling it slides out of the way; then [confirmDismiss] is asked
(false or null brings it back), the root collapses over [resizeDuration]
(a CSS transition of a grid track) and [onDismissed] runs once, with the
direction. The state removes the item (a `Watch.list` row leaves the list);
a Dismissible that was dismissed and kept stays collapsed, as in Flutter.

Keyboard (WCAG 2.5.1 and 2.1.1: a path gesture needs another way): the
root can be focused and Delete or Backspace dismisses it (Shift+arrow along
the axis too), which `aria-keyshortcuts` says; focus moves to the next row,
so it never lands on the page. A keystroke in a text field inside it is the
field's. Offer a visible button for the same action as well.

`// web:` the callbacks are methods of a `ThorState`, not closures:
[onDismissed] gets the [DismissDirection], [confirmDismiss] returns a
`bool` or a `Future<bool>`. Flutter's per-frame `onUpdate` and `onResize`,
`crossAxisEndOffset` and `dragStartBehavior` have no equivalent. Without
JavaScript it is only the child (nothing swipes): give the same action to a
button or a form. The child's own `translate` is replaced while it moves.

constructors.name: Dismissible
constructors.signature:

  required Key key,
  required Widget child,
  Widget? background,
  Widget? secondaryBackground,
  FutureOr<bool?> Function(DismissDirection)? confirmDismiss,
  void Function(DismissDirection)? onDismissed,
  DismissDirection direction = DismissDirection.horizontal,
  Duration? resizeDuration = const Duration(milliseconds: 300),
  Map<DismissDirection, double> dismissThresholds = const {},
  Duration movementDuration = const Duration(milliseconds: 200),
  HitTestBehavior? behavior,
})
constructors.summary: Dismisses [child] when it is dragged away.

params.name: child
params.doc: The widget that slides.

params.name: background
params.doc: Shown under the child while it moves toward [DismissDirection.startToEnd] or down; also for the other directions when there is no [secondaryBackground].

params.name: secondaryBackground
params.doc: Shown under the child while it moves toward [DismissDirection.endToStart] or up.

params.name: confirmDismiss
params.doc: Asked after the child slid out: true dismisses it, false (or null) brings it back. A method of a `ThorState` returning a `bool` or a `Future<bool>`.

params.name: onDismissed
params.doc: Called once the child is dismissed (after the collapse), with the direction it left in. A method of a `ThorState`.

params.name: direction
params.doc: The directions it can be dragged in.

params.name: resizeDuration
params.doc: How long the root takes to collapse once the child is gone, or null to call [onDismissed] right after it slid out.

params.name: dismissThresholds
params.doc: The fraction of the child's size it must be dragged by, per direction (0.4 where none is given).

params.name: movementDuration
params.doc: How long the child takes to slide out (or back).

params.name: behavior
params.doc: Accepted for Flutter's API; the root is the hit target.

name: DragTarget
summary: Flutter's `DragTarget`: where a [Draggable] of the same type can be dropped.
doc:
Flutter's `DragTarget`: where a [Draggable] of the same type can be
dropped.

```dart
DragTarget<String>(
  onWillAcceptWithDetails: board.fits.withArg(column.id),   // bool fits(String column, String task)
  onAcceptWithDetails: board.moved.withArg(column.id),      // void moved(String column, String task)
  overStyle: const StyleProps(outline: BorderSide(color: Color(0xFF2563EB), width: 2)),
  builder: (context, candidates, rejected) => ColumnView(column),
)
```

The target is the element [builder] returns. Draggables are found by
hit-testing under the pointer, and a draggable fits when its type does
(`DragTarget<Object>` takes any, `num` an `int` or a `double`) and
[onWillAcceptWithDetails] (a state method returning a `bool`; true when
there is none) says so.

`// web:` [builder] runs once, on the server, with no candidates: what
changes while a draggable is over the target is CSS ([overStyle] while one
that fits is over it, [rejectStyle] while one that does not is). The
callbacks are methods of a `ThorState` and get the data (text,
a number, an enum value) rather than a details object; [onMove] gets only
the pointer's position inside the target (a state method takes at most three
parameters: with `withArg` that is the argument and the two numbers; the
state knows what is dragged from the draggable's `onDragStarted`).

  Key? key,

  bool Function(T)? onWillAcceptWithDetails,
  void Function(T)? onAcceptWithDetails,
  void Function(T)? onLeave,
  void Function(double, double)? onMove,
  StyleProps? overStyle,
  StyleProps? rejectStyle,
})
constructors.summary: Takes the drops of a [Draggable]`<T>`.

params.name: builder
params.doc: Builds the target (once: see the class).

params.name: onWillAcceptWithDetails
params.doc: Whether a draggable with this data can be dropped here. A state method returning a `bool`.

params.name: onAcceptWithDetails
params.doc: Called when a draggable is dropped here, with its data.

params.name: onLeave
params.doc: Called when a draggable that was over this target leaves it.

params.name: onMove
params.doc: Called (at most once per frame) while a draggable that fits moves over this target, with the pointer's place inside it.

params.name: overStyle
params.doc: Applied while a draggable that fits is over the target.

params.name: rejectStyle
params.doc: Applied while a draggable that does not fit is over the target.

name: Draggable
summary: Flutter's `Draggable`: a widget that can be dragged to a [DragTarget].
doc:
Flutter's `Draggable`: a widget that can be dragged to a [DragTarget].

```dart
Draggable<String>(
  data: task.id,
  feedback: TaskCard(task),
  childWhenDragging: Opacity(opacity: 0.3, child: TaskCard(task)),
  onDragCompleted: board.picked.withArg(task.id),
  child: TaskCard(task),
)
```

Pointer events (not the HTML5 drag-and-drop, which a finger cannot do): the
[feedback] is cloned from a `<template>` as a fixed element under the
pointer and moved with a CSS `translate` (no Dart per frame), the targets
under it are found by hit-testing and the page scrolls when the pointer is
near its edge. [data] reaches the target's state methods as text: a
`String`, a number, a `bool` or an enum value as itself, a `Map` or a `List`
as a JSON `String`. The callbacks are methods of a `ThorState`.

Keyboard (WCAG 2.5.7 and 2.1.1: a drag needs another way): the draggable
can be focused; Space or Enter picks it up, the arrow keys (and Tab) move
between the targets that fit it, Space or Enter drops it, Escape cancels.
A live region says each step ([labels] changes the words).

`// web:` the per-frame `onDragUpdate` and `rootOverlay`,
`ignoringFeedbackSemantics`, `dragAnchorStrategy`s of your own and
`maxSimultaneousDrags` beyond 1 have no equivalent: one drag runs at a
time. The feedback has `position: fixed` and no size of its own: give it
the one it should have. Without JavaScript nothing drags.

name: Drawer
summary: Flutter's `Drawer`: a side panel over the page, on a native modal `<dialog>` (focus trap, Esc and a click on the backdrop close it; no JS). It slides in on open (`@starting-style`). Open it with a `DialogTrigger(id: id, …)` button and close it with `DialogClose`, or from a state method with a [controller] (`details.open()`).
doc:
Flutter's `Drawer`: a side panel over the page, on a native modal
`<dialog>` (focus trap, Esc and a click on the backdrop close it; no
JS). It slides in on open (`@starting-style`). Open it with a
`DialogTrigger(id: id, …)` button and close it with `DialogClose`,
or from a state method with a [controller] (`details.open()`).

With [permanentFrom] it is also Material 3's *standard* drawer: the same
subtree is that modal panel below the breakpoint and an inline panel from
it up, so a filter list is written once.

```dart
Row(
  children: [
    Drawer(id: 'filters', permanentFrom: WindowSizeClass.medium, child: Filters()),
    Expanded(
      child: Column(children: [
        DialogTrigger(id: 'filters', hiddenFrom: WindowSizeClass.medium,
            child: TextButton(child: Text('Filters'))),
        Results(),
      ]),
    ),
  ],
)
```

`// web:` Flutter opens it with `Scaffold.of(context).openDrawer()`;
here any button can open it by id, and a state method through its
`DialogController`.

doc:
Flutter's `DrawerHeader`: the block at the top of a [Drawer], 160 px
tall, with [child] at the bottom start and a divider underneath.

```dart
Drawer(child: ListView(padding: EdgeInsets.zero, children: [
  DrawerHeader(
    decoration: BoxDecoration(color: primary),
    child: Text('Menu'),
  ),
  ListTile(title: Text('Settings'), onTap: settings.open),
]))
```

`// web:` [duration] and [curve] are accepted and ignored: Flutter
animates a change of [decoration] and the browser swaps it at once (a
state that changes it would need a CSS transition, which the server does
not generate). There is no status bar inset (the `<dialog>` is the
viewport); the [Drawer]'s own `padding` (16 by default, unlike Flutter's)
still surrounds the header: pass `padding: EdgeInsets.zero` to the
drawer for an edge-to-edge one. The divider is 1 px of the theme's
outline-variant, or the bottom side of a [decoration] with a border.

name: DropdownMenu
summary: Flutter's `DropdownMenu<T>` (Material 3): a button that opens a list of entries to pick one from, with type-ahead and an optional filter field. A styled select: every part takes the app's look, unlike a native `<select>` (`DropdownButton`).
doc:
Flutter's `DropdownMenu<T>` (Material 3): a button that opens a list
of entries to pick one from, with type-ahead and an optional filter
field. A styled select: every part takes the app's look, unlike a
native `<select>` (`DropdownButton`).

The list is a popover anchored under the button (light dismiss and
Esc are native); the engine's `DropdownMenuFeature` (added by the build
when an app uses `DropdownMenu(`) highlights and picks entries with the
keyboard and the pointer, filters as the user types, and updates the
button. The page ships the engine for it even without a `ThorState`.

Forms: with [name], a hidden `<select>` carries the picked value (the
[initialSelection] at first), so a plain POST works. Without JS that
same `<select>` is the control (`@media (scripting: none)`): the page
stays usable.

Accessibility: the button is a `combobox` with `aria-expanded` and
`aria-controls`; entries are `option`s with `aria-selected`; the
highlighted one is announced through `aria-activedescendant`, on the
button or on the filter field, where focus stays.

```dart
DropdownMenu<String>(
  name: 'fruit',
  initialSelection: 'apple',
  onSelected: order.setFruit,       // void setFruit(String? fruit)
  enableFilter: true,
  dropdownMenuEntries: const [
    DropdownMenuEntry(value: 'apple', label: 'Apple'),
    DropdownMenuEntry(value: 'banana', label: 'Banana'),
  ],
)
```

doc:
`// web:` not in Flutter (it has no attributes): sets attributes on the
element of [child], with no element of its own.

```dart
ElementAttributes(
  HtmlAttributes(data: {'track': 'cta', 'track-id': 'hero'}),
  child: Semantics(role: SemanticsRole.listItem, child: Link(…)),
)
```

For analytics markers, test hooks and `aria-*` that [Semantics] does not
cover. It fuses into the element, so a `data-*` on a list item keeps the
`<li>` (a wrapper element would break the list). An attribute the element
already has is replaced by this one; `class`, `style` and event handlers
are refused by [HtmlAttributes]. For values that change on the page use
`WatchAttributes`.

name: ElementVariables
summary: `// web:` not in Flutter (it has no style cascade): sets custom properties (`--accent`) on the element of [child], from values the server knows (a store's color, a size from data).
doc:
`// web:` not in Flutter (it has no style cascade): sets custom
properties (`--accent`) on the element of [child], from values the server
knows (a store's color, a size from data).

```dart
const accent = CssVariable<Color>('--accent');

ElementVariables(
  {accent: Color(store.primaryColor)},
  child: Card(child: …), // a stylesheet rule reads var(--accent)
)
```

The value reaches the element's one class (the same for every element
with the same value), so the client writes no style; a rule written once
reads it with `Color.variable(accent)` or `Length.variable(gutter)`, and
the descendants inherit it. A value is a [Color], a [Length] or a number;
a value that follows a `ThorState` is `WatchVariables`.

web: tiles with the same [name] form an exclusive accordion (only one

[onExpansionChanged] is a method of a `ThorState` that gets `true` when
the tile opens and `false` when it closes, from the native `toggle`
event of `<details>`: a click, the keyboard or the accordion closing
its sibling all report, and a burst of toggles reports the last state

reported before the one that opens, whatever order the browser sent the
events in. The tile opens and closes without JS; the state only
hears about it once the engine is loaded (the tile's own click loads

```dart
)
```

name: FlutterView
summary: A region of the page drawn by a Flutter web app ("hybrid mode"): a chart, an editor or a game inside an otherwise thor (HTML) page.
doc:
A region of the page drawn by a Flutter web app ("hybrid mode"): a
chart, an editor or a game inside an otherwise thor (HTML) page.

The server renders a sized box with [placeholder] in it, so the page is
complete without Flutter (and without JS). A small inline loader then
mounts the view on its [loading] trigger: the first view downloads the
Flutter build at [src] (see `thor build` and the guide), which starts
**one** engine in multi-view mode; every [FlutterView] of the page is a
view of that app, with its own [initialData]. The placeholder stays
until the view paints its first frame.

```dart
FlutterView(
  src: '/flutter/',
  initialData: {'view': 'chart', 'values': [3, 5, 2]},
  aspectRatio: 16 / 9,
  placeholder: Center(child: Text('Loading the chart…')),
  semanticLabel: 'Sales by month',
)
```

The box never changes size when Flutter arrives (no layout shift): give
it a [height] or an [aspectRatio]; its width is [width] or the whole
width available.

`// web:` Flutter has no counterpart (it is the inverse of
`HtmlElementView`); the name follows `dart:ui`'s `FlutterView`, the
surface a Flutter app draws into.

constructors.name: FlutterView
constructors.signature:
FlutterView({
  Key? key,
  String src = '/flutter/',
  Object? initialData,
  Widget? placeholder,
  double? width,
  double? height,
  double? aspectRatio,
  FlutterViewLoading loading = FlutterViewLoading.visible,
  String? semanticLabel,
  void Function(String)? onMessage,
})
constructors.summary: Creates a view of the Flutter build at [src].

params.name: src
params.doc: Base URL of the Flutter web build (the folder with `flutter_bootstrap.js`). Every [FlutterView] of a page must use the same one: a page runs one Flutter engine.

params.name: initialData
params.doc: JSON-encodable data the Flutter side reads for this view (`ui_web.views.getInitialData(viewId)`); `null` sends nothing.

params.name: placeholder
params.doc: Shown until the view paints its first frame, and for good when there is no JS or the build fails to load. It fills the box.

params.name: width
params.doc: Width in logical pixels (at most the available width); `null` takes the available width.

params.name: height
params.doc: Height in logical pixels. Either this or [aspectRatio] is required: a Flutter view can't size itself to its content.

params.name: aspectRatio
params.doc: Width / height, used when [height] is null.

params.name: loading
params.doc: When the view downloads Flutter and mounts.

params.name: semanticLabel
params.doc: Accessible name of the region (`role="region"`). Flutter's own semantics tree goes inside it.

params.name: onMessage
params.doc: Called with each message the Flutter side sends (a JSON string). A method of a `ThorState` runs in the browser; messages sent before the page's engine is running are dropped.

name: Form
summary: Flutter's `Form` → a native `<form>`: the browser checks every field's rules on submit (focusing the first invalid one), with or without JS.
doc:
Flutter's `Form` → a native `<form>`: the browser checks every field's
rules on submit (focusing the first invalid one), with or without JS.

The form posts to an action method of the page: [onValid]
receives the values of [schema] already checked on the server (an
invalid form re-renders with `422` and the method never runs); [onPost]
takes only the request. Both are tear-offs of the page's methods, and
[S] makes the compiler check that the method takes this schema's
values:

```dart
Form(schema: ContactForm.schema, onValid: send, child: …)
Form(onPost: favorite, child: …)
```

With thor_engine, [onSubmit] (a `ThorState` method) runs instead of
posting (only when every field is valid). Without JS the form posts.

constructors.name: Form
constructors.signature:
Form({
  Key? key,
  required Widget child,
  S? schema,
  FutureOr<ActionResult?> Function(PageRequest, FormValues<S>)? onValid,
  FutureOr<ActionResult?> Function(PageRequest)? onPost,
  void Function()? onSubmit,
  String? action,
  FormMethod? formMethod,
  FormEncoding encoding = FormEncoding.urlEncoded,
  bool disableOnSubmit = true,
  bool resetScroll = false,
  Object? failed,
  Object? defaults,
  bool noValidate = false,
  bool preserveQuery = true,
  bool stay = false,
  ConfirmSpec? confirm,
  String? id,
  String? live,
  Duration liveDelay = const Duration(milliseconds: 350),
})
constructors.summary: Creates a form.

params.name: child
params.doc: The form's fields and controls.

params.name: schema
params.doc: The fields [onValid] receives: the same schema the server checks before running it (`TextFormField(field:)` puts the same rules in the browser).

params.name: onValid
params.doc: The page's action method that receives the checked values: `Future<ActionResult?> send(PageRequest request, FormValues<S> values)`.

params.name: onPost
params.doc: The page's action method that takes only the request: `Future<ActionResult?> favorite(PageRequest request)`.

params.name: onSubmit
params.doc: Run on a valid submit instead of posting: a `ThorState` method (`signup.send`), in the browser.

params.name: action
params.doc: Where the form posts (a URL: another page, `mailto:`). With [onValid] or [onPost], the page whose method it is (`action: articleRoute.link(…), onPost: const ArticlePage().favorite`). A `'?/name'` string is the old, unchecked form of [onPost].

params.name: formMethod
params.doc: The HTTP method the plain-HTML submit uses: [FormMethod.post] (the default) or [FormMethod.get] (a search or a filter: the fields go in the URL).

params.name: encoding
params.doc: `// web:` how the browser encodes what it sends: [FormEncoding.multipart] to send files ([FileField]). A `mailto:` [action] goes as `text/plain` on its own, so the mail client keeps the body.

params.name: disableOnSubmit
params.doc: `// web:` whether a submit marks the form as sending: it gets `data-pending` and `aria-busy="true"` and its submit buttons are disabled until the next page arrives (no double submit; the pressed button's name and value still go). Flutter has no submit to wait for. Turn it off for a form whose answer stays on the page (a download): with no navigation, nothing tells the page it is done.

params.name: resetScroll
params.doc: Start at the top when the answer is this same page. By default a post the page answers (itself, a `422`, a redirect to its path) keeps the scroll and the pressed button; set it for a form that starts the page over (a filter reset, back to page 1). The per-redirect way is `Redirect(url, resetScroll: true)`.

params.name: failed
params.doc: What the page's action answered after a failed submit (`state.form`): the named fields below refill with what was sent and show their messages, with no `value:` or `errorText:` on each. Anything that is not a `FormInvalid` (a `ActionResult.success` data) is ignored.

params.name: defaults
params.doc: The saved values of an edit form: a `Map` by field name or an object with `toJson()` (a model). What was sent ([failed]) wins; a field's own `initialValue` wins over these. THOR-P030 for anything else.

params.name: noValidate
params.doc: `// web:` skips the browser's own bubbles on submit (`novalidate`), so the messages of the server show in the page. Flutter's `Form` has no browser validation to skip. The rules still run on the server.

params.name: preserveQuery
params.doc: `// web:` whether the form keeps the page's query string when it posts to one of the page's actions (`?tab=account&/save`, not `?/save`, which replaces the whole query and lands the answer on the wrong tab or page). On by default; the answer of a failed post never carries the previous action key. Only for [onValid] / [onPost] with no [action] of its own.

params.name: stay
params.doc: Save where the page stands. With JavaScript the form posts without navigating: its submit buttons are disabled while it goes (`data-pending` on the form), the action's `Redirect.back(request).flash(…)` (or a failed `ActionResult`) shows as the page's toast, the files chosen are cleared and the page's server queries are asked again. The action is the same: it still answers a `Redirect`, so without JavaScript the form posts, the browser follows the `303` and the next page shows the flash.

params.name: confirm
params.doc: Ask before the form submits (`onPost`, `onValid`, `action` or `onSubmit`): the page's one native `<dialog>` shows the question and the form goes only on a yes. Without JavaScript it goes straight (see `FilledButton(confirm:)`).

params.name: id
params.doc: The form's `id`, for a button that submits it from outside (`FilledButton(formId: 'filters')`): the footer of a `Dialog` or a `Drawer` sits outside the form it closes. Unique in the page.

params.name: live
params.doc: The id of a `Region` this form keeps up to date as it changes, with no reload: a search box over a server-drawn list. [FormMethod.get] only. After [liveDelay] without typing (and at once on Enter or a change of a select or a checkbox) the browser asks the page for the region with the form's fields as the query, puts the answer in the region and writes the same query in the address bar (`replaceState`: no new history entry). The fields stay where they are, so the caret and the focus are kept: keep the form outside the region. Without JavaScript the form submits and the page loads whole with the same query.

params.name: liveDelay
params.doc: The pause after the last change before a [live] form asks.

name: FutureBuilder
summary: Flutter's `FutureBuilder`: draws [builder] with the state of [future].
doc:
Flutter's `FutureBuilder`: draws [builder] with the state of [future].

The page goes out at once with what [builder] draws for a future that is
not done (its `waiting` snapshot: a skeleton), and when the future
completes the server sends what [builder] draws for the result, which
replaces it. Nothing else of the page waits for it.

```dart
// ThorPage.load: start the call, don't await it
Home(featured: defer(search(featured)));

// build
FutureBuilder<List<Product>>(
  future: data.featured,
  builder: (context, snapshot) => snapshot.hasData
      ? ProductGrid(snapshot.data!)
      : snapshot.hasError ? const Text('Try again later') : const Skeleton(height: 240),
)
```

`snapshot.hasData` is `false` when the future completes with `null` (as in
Flutter): with a nullable `T`, tell waiting from done with
`snapshot.connectionState == ConnectionState.done`, or the skeleton stays
for good (THOR-R033; `thor dev` and the `future_builder_nullable_has_data`
lint say so).

`// web:` the future comes from `load` (create it there, and wrap it in
`defer` so a failure nobody reads yet is not an unhandled error): one
created in `build` is created again by every draw. A page kept in the
cache (`cache:`), an export and the test client draw once with every
future done. The `<head>` (title, meta, canonical) is written before the
future ends: it can't depend on it. `snapshot.error` is the visitor's
message, never the exception (that goes to `onError`). The builder's
result goes into its place in the page: no `<tr>`/`<td>` as the direct
result inside a table (defer the whole table).

name: GeolocationRequest
summary: Asks the browser for the visitor's position when its child is tapped.
doc:
Asks the browser for the visitor's position when its child is tapped.

```dart
// ViewModel: void found(double latitude, double longitude, double accuracy)
//            void failed(String reason)
GeolocationRequest(
  onPosition: nearby.found,
  onError: nearby.failed, // 'denied', 'unavailable', 'timeout' or 'unsupported'
  child: OutlinedButton(onPressed: null, child: Text('Use my location')),
)
```

`// web:` Flutter has no built-in location (the `geolocator` package
returns a `Future<Position>`); here the tap calls
`navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition`, which asks the visitor and
only works on a secure page. The answer reaches methods of a
`ThorState`: [onPosition] with the latitude, longitude and accuracy (in
metres) and [onError] with the reason. Only a tap asks (a page that asks
at load is refused by most browsers and by most visitors); the position
never travels to the server by itself, so a cached page stays the same
for everyone and the state decides what to do with it (a `query`
argument, a link to `?lat=&lng=`). A second tap while one is waiting is
ignored.

  required Widget child,

name: Gesture
summary: Every touch and mouse gesture in one widget: tap, double tap, long press (hold), swipe (to dismiss), drag and pinch, plus press feedback.
doc:
Every touch and mouse gesture in one widget: tap, double tap, long press
(hold), swipe (to dismiss), drag and pinch, plus press feedback.

```dart
Gesture(
  onTap: inbox.open.withArg(m.id),
  onLongPress: inbox.menu.withArg(m.id),
  onSwipe: inbox.swiped.withArg(m.id),     // void swiped(int id, SwipeDirection d)
  swipe: const Swipe(dismiss: true),
  feedback: const Press(),
  child: MessageTile(m),
)
```

Callbacks are methods of a `ThorState`. While a gesture runs the element
follows the pointer through CSS (no Dart per frame); the method runs once
on release with the result:

| Callback | Method gets |
|---|---|
| `onTap`, `onDoubleTap`, `onLongPress` | nothing (or its `withArg`) |
| `onTapDown`, `onTapUp` | `x`, `y` (pixels from the element's top-left corner) |
| `onSwipe` | the [SwipeDirection] |
| `onDragUpdate` | `dx`, `dy` (pixels moved since the last update) |
| `onDragEnd` | `dx`, `dy` (pixels moved) |
| `onScaleEnd` | the scale |

Keyboard: Enter/Space tap (non-native children get `role="button"`), the
context-menu key and right click are a long press, Delete dismisses,
arrows drag, `+`/`-` zoom.

**Live drags:** with [onDragUpdate] the state follows the pointer (a
column edge bound to a `WatchVariables` width, a splitter): the method
gets the movement at most once per animation frame (moves in between
add up, like Flutter's `DragUpdateDetails.delta` coalesced per frame),
then [onDragEnd] gets the whole displacement. The element itself does
not follow the pointer (the state moves what it must). An arrow key is
one update of [Drag.step] pixels, then the end.

**Where it was tapped:** [onTapDown] and [onTapUp] are Flutter's
`onTapDown`/`onTapUp` with the `localPosition` of their details as two
arguments, so one element can be a canvas (a click adds a circle where it
fell) instead of a grid of buttons. The position is in CSS pixels, from
the element's top-left corner (its border box), and does not undo a
`transform` on it. Enter/Space on the focused element is a tap in its
middle; a tap on a native control inside the element is that control's.

`// web:` a tap fires at once even with [onDoubleTap] (Flutter waits to
tell them apart); the element's own `translate`/`scale` are replaced
while it drags (without [onDragUpdate]), swipes or pinches. Flutter's
`onHorizontalDragUpdate`/`onVerticalDragUpdate` are [onDragUpdate] with
`drag: Drag(axis: …)`.

name: GestureDetector
summary: Flutter's `GestureDetector`: a thin wrapper over [Gesture] with Flutter's names.
doc:
Flutter's `GestureDetector`: a thin wrapper over [Gesture] with Flutter's
names.

```dart
GestureDetector(
  onTap: inbox.open,                 // void open()
  onLongPress: inbox.menu,
  onHorizontalDragEnd: inbox.swiped, // void swiped(SwipeDirection d)
  child: MessageTile(m),
)
```

| Flutter | Here |
|---|---|
| `onTap`, `onDoubleTap`, `onLongPress` | the same ([Gesture.onTap]…) |
| `onTapDown`, `onTapUp` | the same: [TapDownDetails], [TapUpDetails] with `localPosition` |
| `onPanUpdate` | the same: [DragUpdateDetails] with `delta` |
| `onPanEnd` | the same: [DragEndDetails] with `velocity`, `localPosition` and `globalPosition` |
| `onHorizontalDragEnd`, `onVerticalDragEnd` | [Gesture.onSwipe] along that axis, [SwipeDirection] (`start`/`end` for horizontal) |
| `onScaleEnd` | [Gesture.onScaleEnd]: the scale |

web: like everywhere in thor, a callback is a method of a `ThorState`
(not a closure). The details objects carry what the browser reports
(see [Gesture]); the fields it can't know are left out. Callbacks the
browser can't do (`onTapCancel`, `onPanStart`, `onScaleUpdate`…) fail when
the page renders, naming what to use; they are `@Deprecated` in the IDE.
With `onPanEnd` alone the element follows the pointer and returns on
release (`Drag(snapBack: true)`); with `onPanUpdate` it stays put and
the state moves what it must. [behavior] is accepted and not used.

Flutter's `GridView.count` / `GridView.extent` → CSS grid; also
`GridView(gridDelegate:)` and `GridView.builder(gridDelegate:,
itemCount:, itemBuilder:)` with Flutter's delegates, which give the same
CSS.

`GridView.extent` is responsive without any breakpoint code or resize
listener: the columns follow the grid's own width by Flutter's formula
(`ceil(width / (max + spacing))`; the padding is not part of the width),
with one `@container` rule per column count, up to 64 columns or 4096px.

```dart
  gridDelegate: const SliverGridDelegateWithMaxCrossAxisExtent(maxCrossAxisExtent: 240, mainAxisSpacing: 16, crossAxisSpacing: 16),
  itemCount: products.length,
  itemBuilder: (context, i) => ProductCard(products[i]),
)
```

a viewport): `itemCount` is required, and `lazyLayout: true` keeps the
browser from laying out the off-screen ones.

name: Hero
summary: Flutter's `Hero`: an element that travels from one page to the next.
doc:
Flutter's `Hero`: an element that travels from one page to the next.

Give the element the same [tag] on both pages (a list's title and the
detail page's heading) and the browser moves and resizes it between
them during the page's view transition (a `PageTransition`), instead of
fading it with the rest of the page. Without a transition (the app's or
the page's), or in a browser without view transitions, it does nothing.

It adds no element and stays out of the way of the wrappers around it
(a `Padding` still merges into the child): [child]'s element gets
`view-transition-name` (`t-hero-` plus the [tag], escaped) in its
`style` attribute, so its class stays the one every similar element
shares. Two `Hero`es with one [tag] on a page are an error in debug
(THOR-R019); in release the second one is left out, as the browser
would skip the whole transition.

```dart
// The list
Hero(tag: 'article-${a.slug}', child: Text(a.title))
// The article page
Hero(tag: 'article-${a.slug}', child: Text(a.title, style: h1))
```

`// web:` Flutter flies the widget between two routes in memory; here
the browser morphs a snapshot of the element between two documents.
There is no `flightShuttleBuilder` or `createRectTween`.

constructors.name: Hero

params.name: tag
params.doc: Pairs this element with the one of the other page (any value: its `toString()` names it).

name: HiddenField
summary: A value the form posts along with its fields and the visitor never sees: `<input type="hidden">`.
doc:
A value the form posts along with its fields and the visitor never sees:
`<input type="hidden">`.

```dart
Form(
  onPost: save,
  child: Column(children: [
    HiddenField(name: 'productId', value: '$id'),
    TextField(name: 'quantity'),
    FilledButton(buttonType: ButtonType.submit, child: Text('Add')),
  ]),
)
```

`// web:` Flutter keeps a form's state in widgets, so it has no hidden
field; the browser posts the DOM, and this is its way to carry a value the
user does not edit (an id, a CSRF token). For one value tied to a button
`onPost: save.withArg(id)` is shorter. On the server it reads like any
field (`request.form()['productId']`, or a schema field of the same name
in `FormValues`).

name: HoverGroup
summary: Marks its child as a hover group: descendants' `.when(groupHover: …)` apply while the pointer is anywhere over it. No extra node.
doc:
Marks its child as a hover group: descendants' `.when(groupHover: …)`
apply while the pointer is anywhere over it. No extra node.

```dart
HoverGroup(child: Card(child: Column(children: [
  Styled(style: StyleProps().when(groupHover: StyleProps(scale: 1.05)),
      child: Image.network(src)),
  Text(name),
])))
```

With a [name] it is a group of its own (Tailwind's `group/name`):
nested groups are addressed apart, `.when(groupHovers: {'card': …})`
reads the nearest group of that name, and `groupHover` keeps reading the
unnamed one.

```dart
HoverGroup(name: 'card', child: Card(child: HoverGroup(name: 'row', child: Row(children: [
  Styled(style: StyleProps().when(groupHovers: {'card': StyleProps(opacity: 1)}), child: icon),
]))))
```

`// web:` Flutter needs a `MouseRegion` + `setState` for this; here it is
one selector, with no state.

name: HtmlWidget
summary: HTML you do not control (a catalog description, a CMS body, a comment) as safe markup, styled with the theme.
doc:
HTML you do not control (a catalog description, a CMS body, a comment)
as safe markup, styled with the theme.

The [html] goes through [sanitizeHtml] with the [policy] on the server
(the page never carries a script, an event handler or a `javascript:`
URL from it), then is written as the children of one `<div>`. Paragraphs,
headings, lists, links, images and tables get the theme's typography and
colors through descendant rules in the page's stylesheet: no inline
styles, and nothing nested widgets (a `Card` inside the content) can
inherit by accident.

```dart
HtmlWidget(product.description)
HtmlWidget(comment.body, policy: HtmlPolicy(linkTarget: '_blank', nofollow: true))
HtmlWidget(post.body, policy: HtmlPolicy(eagerImages: 1)) // a cover image on top
```

Images load lazily (`loading="lazy"`) except the first
[HtmlPolicy.eagerImages].

web: named after `flutter_widget_from_html`'s `HtmlWidget(html)` (the
most used package of the two; `flutter_html`'s `Html(data:)` would also
collide with `package:thor_ui/html.dart`, the raw elements). Unlike
both, nothing is parsed or laid out in Dart at runtime: the browser
draws the HTML, and `onLinkTap`/`customWidgetBuilder` have no
equivalent (links are `<a href>`).

name: Iframe
summary: Another page inside this one: a web-only widget (Flutter has no equivalent; the nearest is `HtmlElementView`, which also hosts a browser element) that renders an `<iframe>`.
doc:
Another page inside this one: a web-only widget (Flutter has no
equivalent; the nearest is `HtmlElementView`, which also hosts a browser
element) that renders an `<iframe>`.

```dart
SizedBox.expand(
  child: Iframe(src: '/preview', title: 'Canvas'),
)
```

An `Iframe` is **one** element with one class, like any thor widget:
the wrappers around it (`SizedBox`, `Expanded`, `Padding`, `Opacity`…)
fuse into it, so it takes the size they give. Alone it is [width] ×
[height] (the browser's 300 × 150 when neither is given) and, unlike the
browser's, has no border: draw one with `DecoratedBox`.

`// web:` [title] is required, the frame's accessible name (WCAG 4.1.2).
Without JavaScript it still works: the browser loads [src]. The framed
page is another document: nothing of this page's state, styles or engine
reaches it (talk to it with `postMessage` from your own script).

name: InkResponse
summary: Flutter's `InkResponse`: a tap target with hover, focus and pressed feedback.
doc:
Flutter's `InkResponse`: a tap target with hover, focus and pressed
feedback.

web: the feedback is CSS of the child's own element, never a new element
or a ripple: a translucent state layer over its background (`:hover`
only where there is a pointer, `:focus-visible`, `:active`), under its
content. An element with its own `background-image` loses it while a
state shows. Without a tap, double tap or long press it is inert.

The child's element is the tap target. When the child is just text, an
icon or an image, that element is a native `<button>` (keyboard, focus
and semantics for free); otherwise it is a `role="button"` element with
`tabindex="0"` (Enter/Space tap with the engine), because a `<button>`
may only hold text-like content. A child that is a button already keeps
its own semantics. A control inside a boxed child (a `Row` with an
`IconButton`) stays its own `<button>`: thor never nests a `<button>` in
a `<button>`; keep such a control out of the tap target, or expect a
screen reader to announce a button in a button.

  Function? onSecondaryTap,
  Function? onSecondaryTapDown,

  Function? onSecondaryTapCancel,

})

params.name: onTap
params.doc: A tap or click (also Enter/Space).

params.name: onDoubleTap
params.doc: Two taps in a row.

params.name: onLongPress
params.doc: A press held ~500 ms, a right click or the context-menu key.

params.name: mouseCursor
params.doc: The pointer over the element (`cursor`); `pointer` by default.

params.name: containedInkWell
params.doc: Whether the feedback fills the element ([InkWell]) or is a circle inside it.

params.name: highlightShape
params.doc: The shape of the feedback when it is not contained: a circle (a radial state layer; the element keeps its own shape) or a rectangle.

params.name: radius
params.doc: Accepted, not used: the circle takes the size of the element.

params.name: borderRadius
params.doc: Rounds the element's corners, and so the feedback with them.

params.name: customBorder
params.doc: Rounds like this shape (`StadiumBorder`, `RoundedRectangleBorder`); over [borderRadius].

params.name: hoverColor

params.name: autofocus

params.doc: Not supported on the web: use onTap (it fires on the click); the pressed look is highlightColor / splashColor.

params.name: onTapUp
params.doc: Not supported on the web: use onTap (it fires on the click).

params.name: onTapCancel
params.doc: Not supported on the web: use onTap; a tap that leaves the element is not a click in the browser.

params.name: onSecondaryTap
params.doc: Not supported on the web: use onLongPress (a right click and the context-menu key are a long press).

params.name: onSecondaryTapDown
params.doc: Not supported on the web: use onLongPress (a right click is a long press).

params.name: onSecondaryTapUp
params.doc: Not supported on the web: use onLongPress (a right click is a long press).

params.name: onSecondaryTapCancel
params.doc: Not supported on the web: use onLongPress.

params.name: onLongPressUp
params.doc: Not supported on the web: use onLongPress.

params.name: onHighlightChanged
params.doc: Not supported on the web: use highlightColor (the pressed look is CSS :active).

params.name: onHover
params.doc: Not supported on the web: use hoverColor (the hover look is CSS :hover); MouseRegion(onEnter:, onExit:) to run a state method.

params.name: onFocusChange
params.doc: Not supported on the web: use focusColor (the focus look is CSS :focus-visible).

summary: Makes a size container around its child, so descendants can respond to *its* width (`.when(container: {...})`, `GridView.count(containerBreakpoints:)`, `Flex(layoutBreakpoints:)`) instead of the viewport's.
doc:
Makes a size container around its child, so descendants can respond to
*its* width (`.when(container: {...})`,
`GridView.count(containerBreakpoints:)`, `Flex(layoutBreakpoints:)`)
instead of the viewport's.

```dart
LayoutScope(
  child: Container(
    padding: const EdgeInsets.all(8).when(container: {400: EdgeInsets.all(24)}),
    child: content,
  ),
)
```

`// web:` the `LayoutBuilder` of a box: Flutter hands its builder the
parent's constraints and rebuilds when they change; CSS container queries
do the same with no builder and no rebuild, so [LayoutScope] only marks
the box and the values of its descendants carry the widths.

It is a real element: CSS container queries never match the container
itself, only its descendants. Like `LayoutBuilder`, it needs a bounded
width; a scope that sizes to its content (e.g. a non-Expanded child of a
Row) collapses to 0 (reported by the debug inspector).

(`content-visibility: auto`), the page-level version of
`ListView(lazyLayout: true)`. [extentEstimate] is its height until it is
first rendered (then the browser remembers the real one).

Useful for long pages of many sections. `// web:` it also clips the child's own painting
to its box (paint containment), so don't use it on a section whose
glows/shadows overflow, nor on the first screen.

name: LazyPiece
summary: A part of the page the server draws only when the browser asks for it: the lazy content of an accordion, a drawer or a tab, which the page does not carry (a menu with 750 entries, the reviews of a product).
doc:
A part of the page the server draws only when the browser asks for it:
the lazy content of an accordion, a drawer or a tab, which the page does
not carry (a menu with 750 entries, the reviews of a product).

```dart
ExpansionTile(
  title: Text(department.name),
  children: [
    LazyPiece<List<Category>>(
      id: 'branch-${department.slug}',
      load: (request) => categories.branch(department.slug),
      builder: (context, branch) => Column(children: [
        for (final c in branch) Link(href: c.url, child: Text(c.name)),
      ]),
      fallback: Link(href: department.url, child: Text('See all')),
    ),
  ],
)
```

The page has a `<div>` with the [fallback] in it and the URL of the piece.
When the [trigger] happens (the accordion opens) a script asks for it
(`GET` the page's URL plus `thor-piece=<id>`), the server draws the page
as always and answers only this piece: [load] runs, [builder] builds
what it returns where the placeholder was (so the theme, the locale and
the route's scopes are those of the page), with the classes it needs. The
browser puts it in place of the fallback and the states it uses are
bound, like the content of a `FutureBuilder`.

Without JavaScript the page keeps the [fallback]: make it a link to a page
that has the same content (`Link(href: …)`), so nobody misses it. Search
engines see the same, and a failed request leaves it too (the next time
the trigger happens it tries again).

`// web:` Flutter has no counterpart (everything is already on the
device). The page's own `load` runs for the fragment's request too (the
builder needs the page's data in scope): keep it cheap or cached (a page
with `cache:` keeps its fragments too), and leave what is heavy to [load].
The [id] names the piece in the page (`[A-Za-z0-9_-.]`) and must not
repeat. A static export keeps the [fallback] (there is no server to ask).
The piece can use `Watch` and the states of the page; a `query()` or a
`FutureBuilder` in it is waited for (the fragment goes out whole, like a
page that waits), and another `LazyPiece` in it is a piece of its own: its
fallback comes with the outer one and it loads when its trigger happens
(the URL names both: `thor-piece=outer:inner`).

constructors.signature:

  required String id,

  Widget? fallback,

})

params.name: id

params.name: load

params.name: builder
params.doc: Draws the piece with what [load] returned.

params.name: fallback
params.doc: What the page shows until the piece arrives and always without JavaScript: usually a `Link` to a page with the same content.

params.name: trigger
params.doc: What loads it (default: when the accordion, dialog or drawer around it opens).

Flutter's `Link` from `url_launcher`. With [newTab] it opens in a new
tab (`target="_blank"`, `rel="noopener noreferrer"`).


summary: A list of entries always shown, of which one, or several with [multiSelectionEnabled], are chosen: a native `<select size>` (with `multiple`). No JS: the browser gives the keyboard (arrows, Home/End, type-ahead; Shift and Ctrl/Cmd to choose several), and the form sends the chosen values under [name].
doc:
A list of entries always shown, of which one, or several with
[multiSelectionEnabled], are chosen: a native `<select size>` (with
`multiple`). No JS: the browser gives the keyboard (arrows, Home/End,
type-ahead; Shift and Ctrl/Cmd to choose several), and the form sends
the chosen values under [name].

```dart
ListBox<String>(
  items: const [
    ListBoxItem(value: 'es', child: Text('Español')),
    ListBoxItem(value: 'en', child: Text('English')),
  ],
  value: settings.language.value,
  onChanged: settings.setLanguage,        // void setLanguage(String? code)
  semanticLabel: 'Idioma',
)
```

A list that changes (filtered, added to) and a selection that the state
changes too are [ListBox.list].

`// web:` Flutter has no list box: a list with a selection is a
`ListView` of `ListTile(selected:)` rows, each with its own tap. Here it
is the browser's control (ARIA's `listbox`, which names it), with the
API of `DropdownButton` ([value], [onChanged]) for one value and of
`SegmentedButton` ([selected], [onSelectionChanged],
[multiSelectionEnabled]) for several. Its entries are text only, like a
`DropdownButton`'s.

constructors.signature:
ListBox({

name: LoadMore
summary: The next page of a list the server drew, appended to it: the rows of a listing, a "Load more" control after them, and no reload. The page's `load` reads the position (`?cursor=…`) and the page draws its [items] and the [next] cursor; the browser asks for the same page with the next cursor, the server answers only this piece (the next rows and the next control) and the browser puts it where the control was.
doc:
The next page of a list the server drew, appended to it: the rows of a
listing, a "Load more" control after them, and no reload. The page's
`load` reads the position (`?cursor=…`) and the page draws its [items]
and the [next] cursor; the browser asks for the same page with the next
cursor, the server answers only this piece (the next rows and the next
control) and the browser puts it where the control was.

```dart
Grid(
  children: [
    LoadMore(
      id: 'places',
      items: [for (final p in state.data.items) PlaceCard(p)],
      next: state.data.next, // null: the last page, no control
      child: const Text('Load more'),
    ),
  ],
)
```

[child] is the control: a `Text`, a `Container`, a chip (not a button: it
becomes the `<a>`). It is a real link to the same page with `?cursor=…`
(`rel="next"`), so without JavaScript, for a search engine, with a modified
click or if the request fails, the visitor goes to the next page. A
[LoadMoreTrigger.visible] control loads by itself when it nears the
screen (infinite scroll).

[items] and the control are the widget's siblings in its parent: put it in
the `Column`, `Grid` or `Wrap` that holds the rows. The control keeps the
rest of the page's query (`?q=pizza&cursor=…`).

`// web:` Flutter's `ListView.builder` asks the model for more; here the
server draws the rows, the page's `load` runs for each request (keep the
rows' query cheap) and the state of the earlier rows stays in the browser.

summary: Flutter's `MenuAnchor`: a button that opens a menu of [MenuItemButton]s and [SubmenuButton]s, on the Popover API (the same as `PopupMenuButton`): no JS, light dismiss and Esc are native, CSS anchor positioning places the menu under the anchor (flipping where it doesn't fit). Choosing a button item closes it natively; following a link item closes it on the tap ([closeOnNavigate]).
doc:
Flutter's `MenuAnchor`: a button that opens a menu of [MenuItemButton]s
and [SubmenuButton]s, on the Popover API (the same as `PopupMenuButton`):
no JS, light dismiss and Esc are native, CSS anchor positioning places
the menu under the anchor (flipping where it doesn't fit). Choosing a
button item closes it natively; following a link item closes it on the
tap ([closeOnNavigate]).

The anchor is the `builder`'s widget (or [child]), and it must be a
button (`IconButton`, `TextButton`…): it is the popover's invoker. The
builder's `controller` and any handler that uses it are accepted but do
nothing, since the browser opens the menu.

```dart
MenuAnchor(
  builder: (context, controller, child) => TextButton(
    onPressed: () => controller.isOpen ? controller.close() : controller.open(),
    child: const Text('Account'),
  ),
  menuChildren: [
    MenuItemButton(onPressed: account.signOut, child: const Text('Sign out')),
    const MenuItemButton(href: '/orders', child: Text('Orders')),
  ],
)
```

`// web:` not supported yet: `onOpen`/`onClose`, `childFocusNode`,
`consumeOutsideTap`, `clipBehavior` and shortcuts. Without JS the menu is
a disclosure (Tab moves between the items); on a page with the engine
the `menu` part makes it an ARIA `menu` (`menuitem`s) with the arrows,
Home/End, type-ahead and submenu keys of the menu button pattern.

summary: Where a [NativeDraggable] of the same type (or a drag from outside the page that carries one of [acceptMimeTypes]) can be dropped: the browser's own drag and drop, next to [DragTarget].
doc:
Where a [NativeDraggable] of the same type (or a drag from outside the
page that carries one of [acceptMimeTypes]) can be dropped: the browser's
own drag and drop, next to [DragTarget].

```dart
NativeDragTarget<String>(
  onWillAcceptWithDetails: tree.fits.withArg(row.id),
  onAcceptWithDetails: tree.moved.withArg(row.id),
  overStyle: const StyleProps(outline: BorderSide(color: Color(0xFF2563EB), width: 2)),
  builder: (context, candidates, rejected) => RowView(row),
)
```

The target is the element [builder] returns, which runs once on the
server (what changes while a drag is over it is CSS: [overStyle] while one
that fits is over it, [rejectStyle] while one that does not is). A
[NativeDraggable] of this page fits when its type does (`Object` takes any,
`num` an `int` or a `double`) and [onWillAcceptWithDetails] says so. A drag
from outside (files, a link, a native drag of another page) fits when its
`dataTransfer.types` has one of [acceptMimeTypes]; its drop gives the text
of the first of those (so `T` is `String`; `Files` give no text).

`// web:` the callbacks are methods of a `ThorState` and get the data as
text, not a details object (as [DragTarget]'s); [onMove] gets the pointer's
place inside the target at most once a frame.

})

name: NativeDraggable
summary: A widget the browser drags with its own drag and drop (HTML5, the `dataTransfer` the drop receives): web-only, next to Flutter's pointer-driven [Draggable] (Flutter has no equivalent, as its drags never leave the app).
doc:
A widget the browser drags with its own drag and drop (HTML5, the
`dataTransfer` the drop receives): web-only, next to Flutter's
pointer-driven [Draggable] (Flutter has no equivalent, as its drags never
leave the app).

```dart
NativeDraggable<String>(
  data: node.id,
  dataTransfer: {'application/x-editor-node': node.toJson()},
  effectAllowed: DragEffect.copy,
  draggingStyle: const StyleProps(opacity: 0.4),
  child: PaletteItem(node),
)
```

What it is for: a drop **outside this page's widgets**. The data goes to
`dataTransfer`, so a page in an [Iframe] (which a pointer drag cannot
reach: the pointer events go to the frame), another window or the desktop
can read it in its own `drop` event with `getData`. Inside the page, use
[Draggable] (it works with a finger, has a feedback and a keyboard way);
a [NativeDragTarget] takes the drops of this widget in the same page too.

[data] is written under [mimeType]; [dataTransfer] adds more (MIME type →
text). The callbacks are methods of a `ThorState`, like [Draggable]'s:
[onDragEnd] and [onDragCompleted] hear whether anything took the drag from
the browser's `dropEffect` (a drop in a frame counts), [onDraggableCanceled]
where the pointer was.

`// web:` the drag image is the browser's (the element itself; there is no
`feedback`, `childWhenDragging` or `axis`): [draggingStyle] styles the
element while it is dragged. There is no keyboard way (the browser has
none): give the action another way (a click, a menu) as well, WCAG 2.5.7.
Without JavaScript the element still drags (`draggable="true"`) but
carries no data.

name: PageView
summary: Flutter's `PageView`: swipeable full-size pages that snap into place.
doc:
Flutter's `PageView`: swipeable full-size pages that snap into place.

```dart
PageView(children: const [Text('one'), Text('two'), Text('three')])
```

With a `PageController` field of a `ThorState` ([controller]) the state
reads and moves the page, and [onPageChanged] is a method of the state:

```dart
final pages = PageController();
final dot = state(0);
void changed(int page) => dot.value = page;     // PageView(onPageChanged: deck.changed, …)
void next() => pages.animateToPage(pages.page!.round() + 1,
    duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 300), curve: Curves.easeOut);
```

`// web:` the browser does it all with CSS `scroll-snap` (touch, trackpad
and keyboard scrolling, momentum): one element, and each page is the
element of its child (a full-size flex item that snaps to its start). It
works with no JS. Flutter's `PageController` and `onPageChanged` are
Dart objects that read the scroll offset on every frame; here the
controller follows the scroller (its `page` is `offset / size`, tracked,
and `jumpToPage` / `animateToPage` move the browser's scroll), and
[onPageChanged] is told the index (`round(offset / size)`) when a scroll
ends (`scrollend`; where a browser has none, when it has paused for 120
ms), only if it changed: Flutter reports it past the halfway point while
the finger is still down.

name: QueryBuilder
summary: Flutter's `FutureBuilder` for a `query`: [builder] draws the query's [AsyncSnapshot], on the server for the first paint and, in the browser, by switching among the states the server shipped.
doc:
Flutter's `FutureBuilder` for a `query`: [builder] draws the query's
[AsyncSnapshot], on the server for the first paint and, in the browser,
by switching among the states the server shipped.

```dart
QueryBuilder(
  query: cart.lines,
  builder: (context, snapshot) {
    if (snapshot.hasError) return Text('Could not load');
    if (!snapshot.hasData) return const Text('Loading…');
    return Watch(cart.rows, itemKey: cart.lineKey,
        each: (row) => row.text(cart.lineText));
  },
)
```

The states are the query's `phase`: waiting with nothing to show,
waiting with the last value, done, failed and done without data (the
answer was null). [builder] runs on the
server, once per state, so **what changes with the data goes through
the state** (`Watch`, `row.text`, [QueryError]), never through
`snapshot.data` read in the builder: the structure is fixed and only
the bindings move.

A state that needs data is left out when the server has none (the query
failed or hasn't run) unless [initialData] stands in for it: give it
when a first paint that failed must switch to the list after a retry.

`// web:` Flutter's builder runs again in every frame; here it runs on
the server and the browser only switches. Flutter's
`FutureBuilder(future:)` has no equivalent for a query, so this is
named after it (TanStack's `useQuery` states, SWR's `isLoading` /
`isValidating`).

name: RawAutocomplete
summary: Flutter's `RawAutocomplete<T>`: a field with an options view anchored to it, drawn by you ([fieldViewBuilder], [optionsViewBuilder]). Use [Autocomplete] for the Material look.
doc:
Flutter's `RawAutocomplete<T>`: a field with an options view anchored to
it, drawn by you ([fieldViewBuilder], [optionsViewBuilder]). Use
[Autocomplete] for the Material look.

The options view is a native popover (`popover="manual"`, so it sits in
the top layer: no sibling covers it and no `Stack` or `overflow` clips
it) anchored under the field with CSS anchor positioning. The engine's
`AutocompleteFeature` (added by the build when an app uses
`Autocomplete(` or `RawAutocomplete(`) opens it while the field has focus
and there is an option to show, moves a highlight with the arrow keys,
picks with Enter or a click (the field takes the option's text), and
closes on Esc, Tab or a click outside. Without JavaScript the field is a
plain text field and the view stays closed.

```dart
RawAutocomplete<String>(
  textEditingController: search.box,       // TextEditingController field
  focusNode: search.focus,
  optionsBuilder: (v) => const [],
  fieldViewBuilder: (context, controller, focus, submit) =>
      TextField(controller: controller, focusNode: focus),
  optionsViewBuilder: (context, onSelected, options) => Watch.list(
    search.names,
    itemKey: search.nameOf,
    each: (row) => Semantics(
      role: SemanticsRole.option,
      child: row.attribute(AttributeName.href, search.hrefOf, child: Link(href: RouteUrl('#'), child: row.text(search.nameOf))),
    ),
  ),
)
```

`// web:` differences from Flutter's: [optionsBuilder] runs once, at
build; the options view is a widget the page holds, which a `ThorState`
list changes ([AutocompleteOptionsBuilder]); no option is highlighted
until the visitor moves to one, so Enter still submits a typed text
(Flutter picks the first option) unless [highlightFirst] is set.

**A palette (inline):** `inline: true` draws the options in the flow
(a `listbox` where you put the autocomplete, no popover), always visible
while there is an option, and `highlightFirst: true` keeps the first
option active so Enter picks it. With `inline` Esc is not taken by the
list: inside a `<dialog>` one press closes the dialog. Keys, with the
list inline: Up/Down wrap, PageUp/PageDown move a page of options, and
Ctrl or Cmd with Home/End go to the first or last option (plain
Home/End stay the caret's, as in the APG combobox).

name: Region
summary: A part of the page that can be asked for alone: the server draws the page as always and answers only this region (`GET` the page's URL plus `thor-piece=<id>`), and the browser puts the answer in place of the region's content. It is what a live search, a product shown in a dialog or any "update this part" needs, with the page's own `load` and `build` deciding what is inside.
doc:
A part of the page that can be asked for alone: the server draws the page
as always and answers only this region (`GET` the page's URL plus
`thor-piece=<id>`), and the browser puts the answer in place of the
region's content. It is what a live search, a product shown in a dialog or
any "update this part" needs, with the page's own `load` and `build`
deciding what is inside.

```dart
// The page's load reads `?q=`; the region is its results.
Form(
  formMethod: FormMethod.get,
  live: 'results',
  child: TextFormField(name: 'q'),
)
Region(id: 'results', child: ResultsList(state.data)),
```

Without JavaScript the `Form` submits and the page loads whole. What fills
a region from outside: `Form(live:)` (replaces its content as the visitor
types), `Link(fetch:)` (shows another page's region here) and, inside the
region, nothing: it is drawn by the page. The region's content may use
`Watch`, buttons and the states of the page.

A state the region reads keeps the value the page gave it when the region
is swapped, unless [syncState] is true: then the answer also carries the
current value of every state the region reads, and the browser replaces
the ones it has with them (see [syncState]).

`// web:` Flutter has no counterpart. The page's `load` runs for the
fragment's request too (the region needs the page's data in scope): keep it
cheap or give the page `cache:`, which keeps its fragments as well. The
[id] names the region in the page (`[A-Za-z0-9_-.]`) and must not repeat. A
static export draws the content with no region around it.
